```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
options(width = 90, digits = 3)
has_glmmtmb <- requireNamespace("glmmTMB", quietly = TRUE)
```

```{r setup}
library(bmassa)
```

This vignette goes through a real data set from the files of the experiment
to a statistical test: it puts the counts in the tables of *bmassa*, estimates
the biomass of every sample, and tests the effect of a fungicide on it with
a generalized linear mixed model.

The data are those of Amador et al. (2024): 24 outdoor mesocosms of 1230 L
(140 cm in diameter, 80 cm of water) with the communities of two habitats of
the Albufera Natural Park (Valencia, Spain), a eutrophic lake and a water
spring, exposed to the fungicide azoxystrobin (controls and 2, 20 and 200
µg/L, applied twice 14 days apart; three mesocosms each). Phytoplankton,
zooplankton and macroinvertebrates were sampled 7 days before the first
application and 7, 21, 35 and 56 days after it. The package ships the raw
files, under a CC BY 4.0 licence: please cite the article when you use
them.

## The raw files

Four files: the design of the experiment and one table per community, as
the counts were entered, one row per sample and one column per taxon.

```{r files}
path <- function(file) system.file("extdata", "azoxystrobin", file, package = "bmassa")
design <- read.csv(path("design.csv"))
phyto <- read.csv(path("phytoplankton.csv"), check.names = FALSE)
zoo <- read.csv(path("zooplankton.csv"), check.names = FALSE)
macro <- read.csv(path("macroinvertebrates.csv"), check.names = FALSE)
head(design, 4)
phyto[1:3, 1:7]
c(phytoplankton = ncol(phyto), zooplankton = ncol(zoo), macroinvertebrates = ncol(macro)) - 3
```

The phytoplankton are cells per litre and the zooplankton individuals per
litre; the macroinvertebrates are the individuals caught in the two traps
(30 × 10 cm each) of each mesocosm and date. The treatment is `W` for the
eutrophic lake and `S` for the water spring.

## One row per sample and taxon

*bmassa* needs one row per sample and taxon. The tables have no identifier of
the mesocosm: within a day, a treatment and a concentration, the three rows
are the three replicates, always in the same order. `to_long()` stacks the
columns of taxa and numbers the replicates, and the design gives the tank:

```{r long}
to_long <- function(d, broad_group) {
  taxa_cols <- setdiff(names(d), c("Day", "Treatment", "Concentration"))
  replicate <- stats::ave(seq_len(nrow(d)), d$Day, d$Treatment, d$Concentration, FUN = seq_along)
  k <- length(taxa_cols)
  data.frame(day = rep(d$Day, k), treatment = rep(d$Treatment, k),
             concentration = rep(d$Concentration, k), replicate = rep(replicate, k),
             broad_group = broad_group, raw_name = rep(taxa_cols, each = nrow(d)),
             abundance = unlist(d[taxa_cols], use.names = FALSE))
}
long <- rbind(to_long(phyto, "phytoplankton"), to_long(zoo, "zooplankton"),
              to_long(macro, "macroinvertebrate"))
tank <- match(paste(long$treatment, long$concentration, long$replicate),
              paste(design$treatment, design$concentration_ug_L, design$replicate))
long$tank <- design$tank[tank]
long$habitat <- design$habitat[tank]
nrow(long)
head(long[long$abundance > 0, ], 3)
```

## Taxon units

Each column is a taxon unit. Its label is turned into a scientific name and,
where the label says so, a life stage: qualifiers such as "sp", "spp." and
"(lineal)" go, misspellings are corrected, and the larvae and adults of the
water beetles become units with their stage. The nauplii are copepods in
that stage; the water mites (Hydracarina) belong to the order
Trombidiformes, and the small coccal algae are taken as green algae
(Chlorophyta), which overestimates the biovolume of cells under 5 µm.

```{r units}
units <- unique(long[c("broad_group", "raw_name")])
rownames(units) <- NULL
units$taxon_id <- gsub("^_+|_+$", "", gsub("[^a-z0-9]+", "_", tolower(units$raw_name)))
nm <- units$raw_name
units$life_stage <- ifelse(grepl("\\(adult\\)$", nm), "adult",
                    ifelse(grepl("larva", nm), "larva",
                    ifelse(grepl(" pupa$", nm), "pupa",
                    ifelse(nm == "Nauplii", "nauplius", NA_character_))))
nm <- sub(" \\(adult\\)$| larvae$| \\(small larva\\)$| pupa$| \\(lineal\\)$", "", nm)
nm <- sub("(_| )spp?\\.?( [0-9]+)?( \\(small\\))?$", "", nm)
fixes <- c(Dyctiosphaerium = "Dictyosphaerium", Ankystrodesmus = "Ankistrodesmus",
           Chroccoccus = "Chroococcus", Pseudonitzschia = "Pseudo-nitzschia",
           "Coccal < 5 um" = "Chlorophyta", Chidorus = "Chydorus", Leidigia = "Leydigia",
           Ciclopoida = "Cyclopoida", Nauplii = "Copepoda",
           "Brachionus havanensis" = "Brachionus havanaensis",
           Orthocladineae = "Orthocladiinae", "Physella Acuta" = "Physella acuta",
           Hydracarina = "Trombidiformes")
fix <- nm %in% names(fixes)
nm[fix] <- fixes[nm[fix]]
units$scientific_name <- nm
changed <- units$scientific_name != units$raw_name | !is.na(units$life_stage)
units[changed, c("raw_name", "scientific_name", "life_stage")][1:12, ]
```

Three labels are left out: *Vorticella*, a ciliate counted both in the
phytoplankton and in the zooplankton; "Coccal colony", which names no taxon;
and *Pleurogyra*, which is not in the Catalogue of Life and has no
classification to estimate it from.

```{r drop}
left_out <- c("Vorticella", "Coccal colony", "Pleurogyra")
units <- units[!units$raw_name %in% left_out, ]
nrow(units)
```

## Classification

`standardize_taxa()` gives each name the classification of the Catalogue of
Life (COL XR), which the models use. A first run reported in `note` that
*Anisoptera*, the dragonflies, is also a genus of bush crickets (which it
took), and that the COL XR has no *Cyclopoida*, *Calanoida* or *Hirudinea*.
The order of the dragonflies tells the homonyms apart, and the
classification given is kept for the names that are not found:

```{r hints}
hints <- data.frame(
  raw_name = c("Zygoptera", "Anisoptera", "Ciclopoida", "Calanoida", "Hirudinea"),
  phylum = c("Arthropoda", "Arthropoda", "Arthropoda", "Arthropoda", "Annelida"),
  class = c("Insecta", "Insecta", "Copepoda", "Copepoda", "Clitellata"),
  order = c("Odonata", "Odonata", "Cyclopoida", "Calanoida", NA))
k <- match(units$raw_name, hints$raw_name)
for (col in c("phylum", "class", "order")) units[[col]] <- hints[[col]][k]
```

`standardize_taxa()` needs internet, so the vignette reads its result, kept
with the data (run on 2026-11-07):

```{r standardize, eval = FALSE}
taxa <- standardize_taxa(units[c("taxon_id", "broad_group", "scientific_name", "phylum",
                                 "class", "order")])
```

```{r standardize-stored}
taxa <- read.csv(path("taxa.csv"), colClasses = "character")
unique(stats::na.omit(taxa$col_release))
taxa[!is.na(taxa$note), c("scientific_name", "col_name", "family", "note")][1:5, ]
```

```{r check-stored, include = FALSE}
# The stored classification is that of these units.
stopifnot(identical(taxa$taxon_id, units$taxon_id),
          identical(taxa$scientific_name, units$scientific_name))
```

The rest of the notes are homonyms in other groups (*Cosmarium* is also a
genus of plants). The stages and the counting units complete the table of
taxa:

```{r taxa}
taxa$life_stage <- units$life_stage
taxa$count_unit <- ifelse(taxa$broad_group == "phytoplankton", "cell", "individual")
```

`check_coverage()` shows from which level of the reference each unit will
be estimated, and how wide its interval will be (the factor by which the
median is divided and multiplied for the 95 % interval of a new population):

```{r coverage}
check_coverage(taxa)
```

There are no lengths, so the intervals are those of typical masses: about
×/÷ 12-23 for a genus or a family, and wider for the units known only at a
higher rank, such as the ostracods, the nauplii and the shrimp *Dugastella
valentina*, from their class. The copepods without a stage are taken as
adults (see below).

## Sampling effort and a common basis

The abundance table has one row per sample and taxon: the tank as `site`,
the day as `date`, and in `per` what each abundance refers to, that is, how
much was sampled. The plankton are densities per litre (`"L"`). The
macroinvertebrates were counted in two traps of 30 × 10 cm per mesocosm and
date, so their `per` is the area of the two traps, `"600 cm2"`. A zero is a
taxon looked for and not found, and its biomass is zero. The habitat and the
concentration go along with the rows.

```{r abundance}
keep <- long$raw_name %in% units$raw_name
ab <- data.frame(site = long$tank, date = long$day,
                 taxon_id = units$taxon_id[match(paste(long$broad_group, long$raw_name),
                                                 paste(units$broad_group, units$raw_name))],
                 abundance = long$abundance,
                 per = ifelse(long$broad_group == "macroinvertebrate", "600 cm2", "L"),
                 habitat = long$habitat, concentration = long$concentration)[keep, ]
head(ab, 3)
```

Densities per litre and per pair of traps cannot be compared or added up.
Given the size of each mesocosm, `convert_abundance()` takes them all to the
whole mesocosm (`"site"`): the two traps are 3.9 % of the bottom of a tank
and a litre 0.081 % of its water, and `per_assumption` says so; the density
of the sample is taken as that of the whole tank.

```{r basis}
tanks <- data.frame(site = design$tank, area = design$area_m2, area_unit = "m2",
                    volume = design$volume_L, volume_unit = "L")
ab_tank <- convert_abundance(ab, to = "site", sites = tanks)
unique(ab_tank[c("per_original", "per", "per_factor", "per_assumption")])
```

## Biomass

All the estimates come in wet mass (mg) by default, here per mesocosm:

```{r estimate}
est <- estimate_biomass(ab_tank, taxa)
est
```

The biomass of each community in each sample, by simulation: the taxa
estimated from the same node of the reference share their errors, and so do
the samples of a taxon (`population_effect = "shared"`), whose population is
the same in all the mesocosms.

```{r totals}
tot <- summarize_biomass(est, by = c("site", "date", "broad_group", "habitat", "concentration"),
                         seed = 1)
tot[1:3, c("site", "date", "broad_group", "biomass_unit", "biomass_median", "biomass_lower",
           "biomass_upper")]
```

A few taxa make most of the biomass of each community (shares of the biomass
of the samples after the first application, with the median mass of each
taxon):

```{r composition}
e <- as.data.frame(est)
after <- e[e$date > 0, ]
after$b <- after$abundance * after$ind_median
share <- stats::aggregate(b ~ broad_group + habitat + taxon_id, data = after, FUN = sum)
share$share <- stats::ave(share$b, share$broad_group, share$habitat, FUN = function(x) x / sum(x))
share <- share[order(share$broad_group, share$habitat, -share$share), ]
do.call(rbind, lapply(split(share, list(share$broad_group, share$habitat)), head, 3))[
  , c("broad_group", "habitat", "taxon_id", "share")]
```

```{r plot-biomass, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4, fig.alt = "Zooplankton biomass per mesocosm (log scale) against the azoxystrobin concentration, in the two habitats, after the first application: lower biomass at the highest concentrations, above all in the eutrophic lake"}
z <- tot[tot$broad_group == "zooplankton" & tot$date > 0, ]
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
for (h in c("eutrophic_lake", "water_spring")) {
  s <- z[z$habitat == h, ]
  x <- match(s$concentration, c(0, 2, 20, 200)) + (match(s$date, c(7, 21, 35, 56)) - 2.5) / 10
  plot(x, s$biomass_median / 1000, log = "y", xaxt = "n", pch = 19,
       col = match(s$date, c(7, 21, 35, 56)), xlab = "Azoxystrobin (µg/L)",
       ylab = "Zooplankton (g per mesocosm)", main = gsub("_", " ", h),
       ylim = range(z$biomass_median / 1000))
  axis(1, at = 1:4, labels = c(0, 2, 20, 200))
}
legend("bottomleft", paste("day", c(7, 21, 35, 56)), col = 1:4, pch = 19, bty = "n", cex = 0.8)
par(op)
```

## Effect of azoxystrobin on biomass

A generalized linear mixed model for each community, with the samples after
the first application: Gamma errors with a log link (biomasses are positive
and their variance grows with the mean), the habitat and the day as fixed
effects with their interaction, a slope of the log concentration
(log10(C + 1)) in each habitat, and the tank as a random effect for its
repeated samples. The R package *glmmTMB* (Brooks et al. 2017) fits it.
`contrasts()` takes the slope in each habitat and their difference, and
`as_ratios()` turns them into ratios: the biomass at a tenfold higher
concentration (of C + 1) relative to that at the lower one, with a 95 %
confidence interval and the p-value of no effect (a ratio of 1). The row
`spring vs lake` is the ratio of the two effects: it tests whether the
habitat changes the effect.

```{r glmm, eval = has_glmmtmb}
d <- tot[tot$date > 0, ]
d$day <- factor(d$date)
d$log_conc <- log10(d$concentration + 1)
glmm <- function(data, y) {
  data$y <- y
  glmmTMB::glmmTMB(y ~ habitat * day + habitat:log_conc + (1 | site),
                   family = Gamma(link = "log"), data = data)
}
contrasts <- function(fit) {
  b <- glmmTMB::fixef(fit)$cond
  v <- stats::vcov(fit)$cond
  k <- c("habitateutrophic_lake:log_conc", "habitatwater_spring:log_conc")
  w <- rbind(eutrophic_lake = c(1, 0), water_spring = c(0, 1), `spring vs lake` = c(-1, 1))
  data.frame(term = rownames(w), estimate = drop(w %*% b[k]),
             variance = diag(w %*% v[k, k] %*% t(w)), row.names = NULL)
}
as_ratios <- function(x) {
  se <- sqrt(x$variance)
  data.frame(term = x$term, ratio = exp(x$estimate), lower = exp(x$estimate - 1.96 * se),
             upper = exp(x$estimate + 1.96 * se), p = 2 * stats::pnorm(-abs(x$estimate / se)))
}
communities <- c("phytoplankton", "zooplankton", "macroinvertebrate")
by_community <- function(f) {
  do.call(rbind, lapply(communities, function(g) cbind(community = g, f(g))))
}
point <- by_community(function(g) {
  dg <- d[d$broad_group == g, ]
  as_ratios(contrasts(glmm(dg, dg$biomass_median)))
})
point
```

## The uncertainty of the masses

The model above takes the biomass of each sample as known, but it comes from
masses with wide intervals. When the fungicide changes the composition of a
community, its effect on the total biomass depends on how heavy the taxa
that change are, which is uncertain. `simulate()` gives joint draws of the
masses: refitting the model to the biomasses of each draw and pooling the
fits with Rubin's rules (the variance of the pooled estimate adds the mean
variance within fits and the variance between them) carries that
uncertainty into the effects. With 30 draws:

```{r draws, eval = has_glmmtmb}
n_draws <- 30
sim <- simulate(est, nsim = n_draws, seed = 1)
draws <- rowsum(e$abundance * sim$ind_mass, paste(e$site, e$date, e$broad_group))
pooled <- by_community(function(g) {
  dg <- d[d$broad_group == g, ]
  bg <- draws[paste(dg$site, dg$date, dg$broad_group), ]
  fits <- lapply(seq_len(n_draws), function(k) contrasts(glmm(dg, bg[, k])))
  m <- sapply(fits, `[[`, "estimate")
  v <- sapply(fits, `[[`, "variance")
  as_ratios(data.frame(term = fits[[1]]$term, estimate = rowMeans(m),
                       variance = rowMeans(v) + (1 + 1 / n_draws) * apply(m, 1, stats::var)))
})
pooled
```

## Numbers and mean mass

The biomass is the number of individuals times their mean mass. The numbers
are counts, not estimates, and the mean mass of the individuals, from
`summarize_size()`, is exact without lengths (the biomass divided by the
individuals; the median and the size classes would be approximations, since
every individual has the mean mass of its taxon). Each taxon keeps its mass,
so a change of the mean mass is a change of composition, towards lighter or
heavier taxa.

```{r numbers, eval = has_glmmtmb}
sz <- summarize_size(est, by = c("site", "date", "broad_group", "habitat", "concentration"),
                     seed = 1)
s <- as.data.frame(sz)
s <- s[s$date > 0, ]
s <- s[match(paste(d$site, d$date, d$broad_group), paste(s$site, s$date, s$broad_group)), ]
numbers <- by_community(function(g) {
  k <- d$broad_group == g
  as_ratios(contrasts(glmm(d[k, ], s$abundance[k])))
})
mean_mass <- by_community(function(g) {
  k <- d$broad_group == g
  as_ratios(contrasts(glmm(d[k, ], s$mean_size[k])))
})
numbers
mean_mass[mean_mass$term != "spring vs lake", ]
```

The snail *Physella acuta* makes more than 80 % of the biomass of the
macroinvertebrates. Its biomass and that of the other macroinvertebrates,
with the median mass of each taxon:

```{r snail, eval = has_glmmtmb}
mi <- after[after$broad_group == "macroinvertebrate", ]
mi$part <- ifelse(mi$taxon_id == "physella_acuta", "Physella acuta", "other taxa")
parts <- stats::aggregate(b ~ site + date + part, data = mi, FUN = sum)
dm <- d[d$broad_group == "macroinvertebrate", ]
snail <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c("Physella acuta", "other taxa"), function(p) {
  bp <- parts[parts$part == p, ]
  cbind(part = p, as_ratios(contrasts(glmm(dm, bp$b[match(paste(dm$site, dm$date),
                                                             paste(bp$site, bp$date))]))))
}))
snail[snail$term != "spring vs lake", ]
```

## Copepods: adults or copepodites?

The cyclopoid and calanoid copepods were counted without their stage, and
*bmassa* takes them as adults. If the counts include copepodites, their
mass, and that of the zooplankton, is overestimated. Taken as copepodites
instead:

```{r copepodites, eval = has_glmmtmb}
taxa_cop <- taxa
taxa_cop$life_stage[taxa_cop$order %in% c("Cyclopoida", "Calanoida")] <- "copepodite"
est_cop <- estimate_biomass(ab_tank, taxa_cop)
e_cop <- as.data.frame(est_cop)
first <- match(c("ciclopoida", "calanoida"), e$taxon_id)
data.frame(taxon_id = e$taxon_id[first], adult_mg = e$ind_median[first],
           copepodite_mg = e_cop$ind_median[first])
tot_cop <- summarize_biomass(est_cop, by = c("site", "date", "broad_group", "habitat",
                                             "concentration"), seed = 1)
zc <- tot_cop[tot_cop$date > 0 & tot_cop$broad_group == "zooplankton", ]
zc <- zc[match(paste(d$site, d$date)[d$broad_group == "zooplankton"],
               paste(zc$site, zc$date)), ]
stats::median(zc$biomass_median / d$biomass_median[d$broad_group == "zooplankton"])
copepodites <- cbind(community = "zooplankton",
                     as_ratios(contrasts(glmm(d[d$broad_group == "zooplankton", ],
                                              zc$biomass_median))))
copepodites
```

## Discussion

```{r discussion-helpers, include = FALSE}
# Ratios and intervals for the text (the tables need glmmTMB).
rc <- function(tab, community, term, col = "community") {
  if (!has_glmmtmb) return("(needs *glmmTMB*)")
  r <- tab[tab[[col]] == community & tab$term == term, ]
  sprintf("%.2f [%.2f-%.2f]", r$ratio, r$lower, r$upper)
}
loss <- function(tab, community, term, steps = log10(201)) {
  if (!has_glmmtmb) return("?")
  r <- tab[tab$community == community & tab$term == term, ]
  round(100 * (1 - r$ratio^steps))
}
p_range <- function(tab) {
  if (!has_glmmtmb) return("?")
  p <- tab$p[tab$term != "spring vs lake" & tab$ratio < 1]
  sprintf("%.2f to %.2f", min(p), max(p))
}
cop_ratio <- if (has_glmmtmb) {
  zc$biomass_median / d$biomass_median[d$broad_group == "zooplankton"]
} else NA
cop_median <- round(100 * (1 - stats::median(cop_ratio)))
cop_max <- round(100 * (1 - min(cop_ratio)))
```

What can be concluded from these models about the effects of azoxystrobin on
the biomass of the three communities, and about the role of the habitat?

**Direction and size of the effects.** In the three communities and in both
habitats, the biomass was lower at higher concentrations. Per tenfold
increase of the concentration, it fell to a ratio (with its 95 % interval)
of
`r rc(point, "phytoplankton", "eutrophic_lake")` in the phytoplankton of the
eutrophic lake, `r rc(point, "zooplankton", "eutrophic_lake")` and
`r rc(point, "zooplankton", "water_spring")` in the zooplankton of the lake
and of the spring, and `r rc(point, "macroinvertebrate", "eutrophic_lake")`
and `r rc(point, "macroinvertebrate", "water_spring")` in the
macroinvertebrates. From the controls to 200 µg/L, 2.3 tenfold steps, the
macroinvertebrates would lose about
`r loss(point, "macroinvertebrate", "eutrophic_lake")` % of their biomass
and the zooplankton of the lake about
`r loss(point, "zooplankton", "eutrophic_lake")` %. Only the phytoplankton
of the water spring showed no clear decline.

**How certain.** These intervals take the biomass of each sample as known.
Once the uncertainty of the masses is carried into the model, the intervals
widen and all of them include 1 (p from `r p_range(pooled)`): the
masses come from typical values of each taxon, not from measurements in
these mesocosms, and the fungicide changed the composition of the
communities, so how much biomass was lost depends on how heavy the taxa that
declined are. The numbers of individuals do not depend on the masses, and
they confirm the declines of the macroinvertebrates in both habitats
(`r rc(numbers, "macroinvertebrate", "eutrophic_lake")` and
`r rc(numbers, "macroinvertebrate", "water_spring")`) and of the zooplankton
and the phytoplankton of the lake
(`r rc(numbers, "zooplankton", "eutrophic_lake")` and
`r rc(numbers, "phytoplankton", "eutrophic_lake")`). The evidence is
therefore firm for the losses of individuals and consistent, but imprecise,
for the losses of biomass. Measuring the lengths of the few animals that
make most of the biomass, the snail *Physella acuta* and the cyclopoid
copepods, would narrow the intervals most.

**The habitat.** The habitat did not change the size of the effects on
biomass detectably: the ratios of the effect in the spring to that in the
lake are close to 1, with wide intervals, in the three communities
(`r rc(point, "phytoplankton", "spring vs lake")`,
`r rc(point, "zooplankton", "spring vs lake")` and
`r rc(point, "macroinvertebrate", "spring vs lake")`). It did change how
the zooplankton lost its biomass. In the lake it lost individuals, with the
same mean mass; in the spring the number of individuals did not change
(ratio of the effects on numbers, spring to lake,
`r rc(numbers, "zooplankton", "spring vs lake")`), but their mean mass fell
(`r rc(mean_mass, "zooplankton", "water_spring")`): the zooplankton of the
spring turned towards lighter taxa, and its biomass fell with them. In the
macroinvertebrates, the snail and the other taxa did not respond alike in
each habitat: in the lake the other taxa declined clearly
(`r rc(snail, "other taxa", "eutrophic_lake", "part")`) and the snail less
(`r rc(snail, "Physella acuta", "eutrophic_lake", "part")`); in the spring
the snail declined clearly
(`r rc(snail, "Physella acuta", "water_spring", "part")`) and the other
taxa less (`r rc(snail, "other taxa", "water_spring", "part")`). A similar
loss of biomass can thus hide different changes in each habitat.

**Composition and biomass.** Amador et al. (2024) analysed the composition of
the communities and found the most sensitive taxa in the water spring: there
the zooplankton changed at the lowest concentration (community NOEC below 2
µg/L on days 7 and 35), and the macroinvertebrates mostly through the decline
of the crustaceans *Echinogammarus* and *Dugastella valentina*. The biomass
adds another view: the change of the zooplankton of the spring was one of
composition, without loss of individuals, and the crustaceans that drove the
change of the macroinvertebrates make little of their biomass, which is
mostly snails.

**Copepods.** The cyclopoid and calanoid copepods were taken as adults, so
the zooplankton biomass may be overestimated if the counts include
copepodites: were all of them copepodites, the biomass of a sample would be
lower by a median of `r cop_median` %, and by up to `r cop_max` % where
copepods dominate. The effect of azoxystrobin does not depend on this
assumption (`r rc(copepodites, "zooplankton", "eutrophic_lake")` and
`r rc(copepodites, "zooplankton", "water_spring")` with copepodites): it
changes how much zooplankton there is, not how it responded.

**Other assumptions.** The macroinvertebrates of each sample come from two
traps of 30 × 10 cm, and their biomass per mesocosm takes the density of the
traps for the whole bottom; this sets the level of the biomass, not the
effects, since all the mesocosms are the same size. The effect of the
concentration is taken as log-linear and constant from day 7 to day 56.

In short, azoxystrobin reduced the number of individuals of the
macroinvertebrates in both habitats and of the zooplankton and the
phytoplankton in the eutrophic lake, with losses of biomass in the same
direction but uncertain in size while the masses come from typical values.
The habitat did not change the size of the effects on biomass detectably,
but it changed their form: the zooplankton of the lake lost individuals and
that of the spring turned towards lighter taxa.
